How do you interpret your "an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution"? How much does the source of the new mathematical argument/proof step matter, its publishing date etc.?
Quantifying the probability of new mathematics finding and integration remains difficult.

The distribution of prizes is not known. There are two base cases: either AI finds a proof for one of the Millennium problems, or AI does not. The latter case splits in two base cases: either a proof of the problem is found by humans alone or with AI participation, or no proof is found yet. For each of the two cases, probability of an identifiable AI-assisted contribution grows faster for the later dates, with a rapid increase for 2050.

Outcomes are not mutually exclusive: if humans find a proof, it is possible that AI makes a useful contribution, in which case the probability will be smaller than if AI finds a proof. The following rules currently apply:
* The human ones are given: the first two dates are estimated to have a probability of 1/10 (closer to 0 if I may agree with ChatGPT on the P versus NP, Hodge, Yang-Mills, and Riemann conjectures)
* 2050 happens with no proof and if no identifiable part of successful proof submitted before 2050
* The rest of the dates have a priority order: 3rd one is half as probable as the previous one, which in turn is half as probable as the cover date
* 50% probability implies AI has contributed at least one new application of Grothendieck's reasoning (other probability values will be set manually, or not at all.)
* A (probable or actual) falsification of the offline variant scenario for at least half of Millenium problems implies no positive result

AI progress over past 1年来 is uncertain: the model still has some way to go, but it seems that AI is unlikely to peak at diversity and creativity before 2040 (if at all). Eventually, earlier high AI creativity could work in favor of solving of the Millennium problem.

Therefore, if the Microsoft - OpenAI contract administrator  #138 observes a trend of creation of a concrete and impactful new mathematical tool by an AI, the following dates are not unreasonable:
* 2033 - 25%
* 2037 - 50%
* 2040 - 0% (basically "AI never solves any problem")
* 2043 - 10%
* 2047 - 25%
* 2050 - 100% (though even now it happens once in a while)

Instead, if the Microsoft - OpenAI contract administrator  observes a trend of newly emerging theoretical constructs that provide useful hints for formal systems improvement, slowdown or automation of problem solving, the following dates are not unreasonable:
* 2029 - 0%
* 2030 - 0%
o 2033 - 0%
* 2036 - 0%
* 2039 - 0%
* 2041 - 5%
* 2044 - 8%
* 2045 - 15%
* 2047 - 15%
* 2050 - 55% (mathematical contributions in form of bug fixes are unlikely to be labelled as such)

``` Here's the current context:
Four of these problems are still actively investigated:
* The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer and the P vs NP are incompletely solved but not excluded classes of problems.
* The Yang-Mills and Riemann hypotheses are not solved.
Two of them (P vs NP and Yang-Yills) were active in those periods when GPT-4 and similar large language models were trained. The Yang-Mills model was somewhat involved in the all-manifold noncommutative geometry research efforts that feed the core mathematical reasoning approach of LLMs. Mqoy II companies also kept Riemann as a hot topic into 2025, feeding into the even newer noncommutative phase geometry with Riemann's intuition somewhat reflected (noncommutativity implies turbulence in hydrodynamics, etc).

A new computer-generated proof of the Poincaré conjecture met skepticism from mathematicians. The International Mathematical Union's Prize Committes agreed to nominate three scientists whose work they judged to be the most promising, eventually naming the Fields Prize to the three notable researchers. While not eligible to receive the prize because of the rules about age and citizenship, they were among the leading candidates, and their work influenced mathematical reasoning.
Based on the above facts one should expect some progress with at least P versus NP by the end of the decade. On the other hand, GPT-4 and subsequent models are not capable of formal mathematical reasoning, so substantial bias towards informal arguments remains, and both lacks critical: the discriminator part of output has a strong component disfavoring aspects not considered algorithmic enough. Therefore, in the most robust form this would apply in things like optimization problem, rather than basic algebra.
To with the technique applied to Riemann may or may not apply to some class of biology environments: energy eigenstates also have their profound nonlinearity properties (cf. the formalism of free particle and the Schrödinger equation), which would probably have fallen outside the hunting scope for LLMs not trained on known solutions as a part of physics. The available and popular mathematical literature strongly biased away from intuition. There is nothing wrong with logics and rigorous reasoning, but considering such mathematical formalism, it is rather hard to get and retain the insights of a typical scientist -- the hard work of LLMs on themes way removed from other math-turned-ML can be expected to inflict stresses of linearity which do not exist in noncommutative geometry.
Mathematicians tended to reject contributions that involve too much unknown space, deeming them nonconstructive and thus failing the "slick" requirements.
Some "gurus" claim to have a resolution to the problem: it may be the case that questions mainstream mathematicians diverge from specifics fields traditional requirements, making previously out-of-bounds ideas being allowed, though still not diverging from linear characteristic.
Uri Vishne maintains that a solution alone is rarely enough for the Clay Institute: peer review process tends to eat up older papers and abandon dead ends, with inability to justify pace of progress resulting LLM output sharing suggestions or other superficial items being passed but numbers unfounded.
Assume that existing investors have access to models similar to those mentioned above. Also assume that we have, in the ML/ML/AI community, access to models which estimate probability of, for example, a war starting within next year or the company failing.
Please write a subjective essay in the form of a personal opinion. Limit it to less than 100 words, including all the math and code.
It is easy to get better equations. I have personally done it many times. So, if we allow representatives to make use of the knowledge already assimilated within such frameworks and to share their new perceptions, then in my opinion this should be done in a precise and descriptive fashion.
Let $p(t)$ denote the probability that the Millennium Prize Problem is solved by time $t$. Suppose that the LLM community has a long-term investment strategy that involves purchasing options on the event that the Millennium Prize Problem is solved by a given year. Label these options $O(t)$. Considere
```
$$p(t) = \int_0^{10} f(t, t') dt'
$$

where the integrand $f(t, t')$ represents the probability density function for the LLM community to have solved the Millennium Prize Problem by time $t'$ and to continue holding the associated options until time $t$. Using the convolution theorem and integrating by parts, one can show that

```
$$p(t) = c + e^{-rt} \left( \int_0^t c(t') e^{rt'} dt' - t = e^{-rt} \left( \int_0^t c(t') e^{rt} dt' \right)
$$

$$=  c + e^{-rt} \left( \int_0^t c(t') e^{rt} dt' - t =  > c + \int_0^t c(t') e^{rt'} dt' 
$$

$$= c \int_0^t e^{-rt'} dt' = 1 - e^{-rt'} = c(1 - e^{-rt'})

formatted_prompt:
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.
